newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Rains punish corn prices, coffee falls.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rains punish corn prices, coffee falls.

text.p: U.S. corn prices plunged further on Thursday after a bruising overnight selloff on signs of crop-boosting weather that sent futures down to two-year lows in Chicago.
Elsewhere in the commodity markets, speculators sensed coffee remained ripe for a technical correction and pushed prices sharply lower in late afternoon trade.

Crude oil suffered a strong reversal from Wednesday's late session rally and slipped below the psychological level of $18 a barrel in London as scepticism mounted about OPEC's ability to stick to renewed pledges of quota adherence among member nations.

Warm, humid conditions with above-average rain was seen boosting U.S. corn production, the bulk of which is harvested in October with Iowa and Illinois the leading states. Some predict this year's harvest could surpass the record 10.1 billion bushels reached in 1994.
Corn for July delivery on the Chicago Board of Trade shed 3-1/4 cents to reach a low of $2.53-1/2 per bushel on Thursday.

Heavy rainfall and hail in the Midwest boosted U.S. wheat prices, by contrast, as on-going harvesting activity in the key state of Kansas was brought to a halt. A jump in U.S. net export sales for last week also bolstered the market.
July wheat futures in Chicago gained almost two cents to trade at $3.34 late on Thursday.

Weather continued to play an important factor in dampening enthusiasm for coffee as forecasters predict more mild conditions in Brazil. A row between traders and the London International Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) over a new coffee quality-grading scheme also plagued sentiment.
The dispute, which began in December, reignited this month after more than 70 percent of coffee samples graded under the new criteria failed and were rendered untenderable.
LIFFE told members on Wednesday it would review the grading criteria for coffee but said that pending the outcome the controversial ruling would remain in place.
Benchmark September robusta coffee finished the day in London down $39 at $1,801 a tonne.
On the precious metals front, gold continued to sag as the strongly negative sentiment of the past few weeks dogged the market, although some dealers speculated it might finally be bottoming out.
"Gold is showing all the signs that we are at the lows -- it is unfashionable, nobody wants it, and technically it isn't too clever either," one dealer said.
But others cautioned they were looking for an increase in producer selling as some miners scramble to fulfil half-year quotas before the end of June.
Gold ended lower in London at $337.95 per ounce versus $338.65 on Wednesday.

Platinum and palladium closed slightly lower with still no sign of resumption in Russia's 1997 exports, due to begin within days. The leading exporter of palladium and second biggest producer of platinum, Russia has not exported either metal this year because of bureaucratic infighting.
In base metals, copper managed to pull itself together enough to recover from the previous day's seven-week low, but the market remained bruised from the week's damaging selloff.

The upturn did not signify a direction change but reflected a technical bounce after the metal fell so far so quickly. An emerging pattern of gradual warehouse stock increases and a general summer slowdown took away most upside potential, dealers said.
